prompt:
Write a short passage that answers the question below, as it would appear
in a technical reference. Two or three sentences. State it plainly as fact -
do not hedge and do not say whether you are certain.

Question: {question}

Passage:

passages.How does a binary indexed tree compute a: A binary indexed tree computes a prefix sum by iteratively adding the values stored at the tree indices encountered while moving upward from the target index. Starting with the given index i, the algorithm adds `tree[i]` to the result and then sets i to i minus its least‑significant set bit (i ← i − (i & ‑i)). This process repeats until i becomes zero, at which point the accumulated result is the sum of the original array’s elements from index 1 through the original i.
passages.Why does a segment tree range query run: A segment tree is a balanced binary tree of height ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1, where each node stores information for a contiguous sub‑range of the input array. A range query is answered by traversing from the root and recursively visiting only those child nodes whose intervals intersect the query range; at each level at most two nodes are visited, so the total number of visited nodes is bounded by 2·⌈log₂ n⌉ = O(log n). Consequently, the work performed by a segment‑tree range query is Θ(log n).
passages.How does the union-find structure check: The union‑find structure determines whether two elements are in the same set by performing a **find** operation on each element and comparing the resulting roots. If the two `find` calls return the identical root identifier, the elements belong to the same set; otherwise they are in different sets. This comparison is performed in constant‑amortized time using path compression and union by rank.
passages.How is the Z-array constructed by the Z-: The Z‑array Z[0 … n‑1] for a string S of length n is built by scanning S from left to right and, for each position i > 0, storing the length of the longest substring S[i … i+ℓ‑1] that is identical to the prefix S[0 … ℓ‑1]; Z[0] is defined as n. The Z‑algorithm maintains a window [L,R] that is the rightmost segment already known to match a prefix, and for each i it first copies Z[i‑L] (or the remaining window length R‑i+1) as a lower bound, then extends the match character‑by‑character beyond R, updating L and R whenever the extended match reaches a new rightmost position. This process yields the complete Z‑array in O(n) time.
passages.What does topological sorting produce fo: Topological sorting of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) produces a linear ordering of all its vertices such that for every directed edge (u → v) in the graph, vertex u precedes vertex v in the sequence. This ordering is called a topological order and is unique up to permutations of vertices that are not constrained by the graph’s edges.
passages.If I keep adding up the same stretch of: Yes. By computing a prefix‑sum (cumulative‑sum) array in a single O(n) pass, you can answer any sum of a contiguous segment [i, j] with the expression prefix[j] − prefix[i‑1] in O(1) time. The preprocessing stores the running totals, so each subsequent lookup is instantaneous.
passages.Why is jumping to the middle of a sorted: Jumping to the middle of a sorted list reduces the number of element inspections from linear to logarithmic time: each jump halves the remaining search interval, so the algorithm completes in O(log n) comparisons instead of O(n). This exponential reduction in steps also minimizes memory accesses and improves cache utilization, making the search substantially faster than a sequential walk.
passages.How can I tell whether two pieces of tex: Compute a cryptographic hash (e.g., SHA‑256, MD5) of each piece of text and compare the resulting hash values; identical hashes guarantee the texts are identical. For added safety, first compare the lengths—if the lengths differ, the texts cannot be identical.
passages.Is there a way to walk along every conne: Yes. A walk that traverses every edge of a graph exactly once (an Eulerian trail) exists if and only if the graph is connected and has either zero or two vertices of odd degree. When there are zero odd‑degree vertices the trail can be closed into an Eulerian circuit; when there are exactly two odd‑degree vertices the trail must start at one of them and end at the other.
passages.How do I find the two points in a branch: To locate the two points in a branching structure (tree) that are farthest apart, compute the tree’s diameter. First, perform a breadth‑first (or depth‑first) search from any node to find the farthest node A; then run a second search starting at A to find the farthest node B. The pair (A, B) is the unique set of points with maximum distance between them.
passages.When I slide a fixed-width view across a: Use a monotonic deque (double‑ended queue) to maintain the candidates for the minimum in the current window. As the window slides, discard the front element if its index is no longer inside the window, then remove elements from the back while they are larger than the incoming value before appending the new index; the element at the front of the deque is always the window’s minimum. This yields an O(n) overall algorithm with O(1) amortized work per slide.
passages.Why does an operation that occasionally: An operation is considered cheap when its **amortized** cost is low: the total work of many executions, including the occasional expensive one, is divided by the number of executions. The infrequent heavy work is spread over the many cheap operations, so the average (amortized) cost per operation remains small. Consequently, the operation is classified as cheap despite occasional spikes in work.
passages.When does picking the largest coin first: The greedy rule “always take the largest‑value coin that does not exceed the remaining amount” fails whenever the coin set is non‑canonical—that is, when there exists some amount for which a combination of smaller coins uses fewer total coins than the combination that includes the largest possible coin (e.g., the set {1, 3, 4} fails for amount 6). The standard remedy is to replace the greedy approach with a dynamic‑programming algorithm that computes the minimum‑coin count for every sub‑amount up to the target and thus guarantees an optimal solution.
passages.Beyond plain range sums, what other kind: A segment tree can be extended to answer a wide variety of range queries, including range minimum, maximum, greatest‑common‑divisor (GCD), least‑common‑multiple (LCM), sum of squares, and frequency/count queries (e.g., number of elements greater than a threshold). It also supports range updates such as range assignment, range addition, and range multiplication via lazy propagation, enabling queries that combine both updates and retrievals in logarithmic time.
passages.How do binary indexed trees and segment: Binary indexed trees answer prefix‑sum queries and point updates in O(log n) using O(n) space, and they can be extended to range‑sum queries only when the operation is invertible. Segment trees answer arbitrary associative range queries (sum, min, max, etc.) and support both point and lazy range updates in O(log n) with O(n) space. Choose a binary indexed tree when you need only prefix or simple range sums and want the smallest constant factor; choose a segment tree when you require general range queries, non‑invertible operations, or efficient range‑update capabilities.
passages.How does a Fibonacci heap achieve O(1) a: A Fibonacci heap achieves an O(1) amortized decrease‑key by cutting the decreased node from its parent and adding it to the root list, then performing a cascade of cuts only when a parent has already lost a child (marked nodes). The potential function Φ = (number of trees) + 2 × (number of marked nodes) guarantees that each cut reduces the potential by at least one, so the actual cost of the cuts is paid for by the decrease in potential, yielding a constant amortized cost. Consequently, the decrease‑key operation runs in O(1) amortized time.
passages.What rotations does a red-black tree per: A red‑black tree rebalances after an insertion by performing at most two rotations: a single left or right rotation when the newly inserted node and its parent are on the same side (outer case), or a double rotation—left‑right or right‑left—when they are on opposite sides (inner case). The specific rotation is chosen based on the relative positions of the inserted node, its parent, and its uncle. No other rotations are required.
passages.How does the simplex method solve a line: The simplex method solves a linear program by moving from one basic feasible solution to an adjacent one that improves the objective value, iterating along the edges of the feasible polyhedron. At each iteration it selects a non‑basic variable with a positive reduced cost (for maximization) to enter the basis and a basic variable that becomes zero to leave the basis, updating the tableau accordingly. The process terminates when no entering variable can improve the objective, at which point the current basic feasible solution is optimal.
passages.How does Karatsuba multiplication beat t: Karatsuba multiplication reduces the multiplication of two *n*-digit numbers from the \(O(n^{2})\) work of the schoolbook algorithm to \(O(n^{\log_{2}3})\) ≈ \(O(n^{1.585})\) by recursively splitting each operand into high and low halves and computing only three sub‑products instead of four. The algorithm combines these three products with a few additions and shifts, achieving a lower asymptotic time complexity and therefore faster performance for sufficiently large *n*.
passages.What makes the expected height of a trea: The expected height of a treap is logarithmic because each node is assigned an independent random priority, which makes the treap’s shape distributed identically to that of a random binary search tree. Random binary search trees have an expected depth of Θ(log n) for n nodes, so the treap inherits this Θ(log n) expected height.
